The Department of the Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service issued a final rule amending 31 CFR Part 356, the Uniform Offering Circular governing auctions of marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.  

The rule makes technical changes to remove outdated references, clarify definitions, and align auction terminology with Treasury’s current practices and planned auction-system upgrades.  

It revises provisions on inflation-protected securities calculations, CUSIP definitions, bid submission, auction awards, and the publication of auction results, while replacing specific references to TreasuryDirect with a general website reference.  

A key operational change requires submitters of noncompetitive customer bids to provide each customer’s name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction closes, eliminating summary bids.  

The rule becomes effective October 15, 2026, with certain changes applying beginning with the first auction conducted on Treasury’s upgraded auction system.

The article presents DiffTry, a mechanism that prioritizes microservice requests during overload by assigning different retry limits to different priority classes.  
Instead of treating all retries equally, it gives high-value requests more attempts while limiting low-priority traffic, reducing retry storms and protecting important transactions.  
The authors develop analytical models for a single service and extend them to general service networks to estimate per-class rejection rates and end-to-end completion probabilities.  
They prove convergence of the network solution, establish uniqueness conditions for many practical DAG-like flows, and show that success rates improve monotonically as retry limits for a class increase.  
Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment validate the approach, demonstrating that DiffTry can be added as a lightweight service-mesh plugin without changing application code.

DiffTry assigns different retry limits to different priority classes.
DiffTry gives high-value requests more retry attempts while limiting low-priority traffic.
DiffTry reduces retry storms and protects important transactions.
The authors of the article develop analytical models for a single service.
The authors extend their analytical models to general service networks.
The analytical models estimate per-class rejection rates and end-to-end completion probabilities.
The authors prove the convergence of the network solution.
The authors establish uniqueness conditions for the network solution in many practical DAG-like flows.
The authors show that request success rates improve monotonically as retry limits for a priority class increase.
Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment validate the DiffTry approach.
DiffTry can be added as a lightweight service-mesh plugin.
Adding DiffTry does not require changing application code.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

The Federal Aviation Administration has adopted a final airworthiness directive amending 14 CFR Part 39 for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes.

The directive addresses reports of low clearance in the right wing between fuel line components, hydraulic system lines, and a fuel vent tube, a condition that could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike.

It requires replacing a harness support bracket clip-nut, replacing certain fuel tube assemblies, inspecting clearance between hydraulic lines and the fuel vent tube, and performing corrective repairs if inadequate clearance is found.

The rule follows a Transport Canada airworthiness directive and was adopted as proposed after commenters generally supported the action or raised issues the agency rejected.

The directive is effective November 18, 2026, and the FAA estimates required actions will cost about $2,693 per airplane, totaling about $161,580 for 60 affected aircraft on the United States registry.

claim_breakdown.claim: The Federal Aviation Administration has adopted a final airworthiness directive amending 14 CFR Part 39.
The FAA's final airworthiness directive applies to certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes.
The directive addresses reports of low clearance in the right wing between fuel line components, hydraulic system lines, and a fuel vent tube.
Low clearance in the right wing between fuel line components, hydraulic system lines, and a fuel vent tube could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike.
The directive requires replacing a harness support bracket clip-nut.
The directive requires replacing certain fuel tube assemblies.
The directive requires inspecting clearance between hydraulic lines and the fuel vent tube.
The directive requires performing corrective repairs if inadequate clearance is found.
The FAA rule follows a Transport Canada airworthiness directive.
The FAA rule was adopted as proposed after commenters generally supported the action or raised issues the agency rejected.
The directive is effective November 18, 2026.
The FAA estimates the required actions will cost about $2,693 per airplane.
The FAA estimates the required actions will cost a total of about $161,580 for the affected aircraft.
There are 60 affected aircraft on the United States registry.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The FAA adopted Airworthiness Directive 2026-20-09 (Amendment 39-23482, Docket No. FAA-2026-2289) for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes, effective November 18, 2026.

The AD was prompted by Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 dated October 1, 2025, which reported low clearance conditions in the right wing between fuel line flexible coupling and harness support bracket clip-nut, between fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between hydraulic system and fuel vent tube.

The AD requires rectifying low clearance conditions between fuel line flexible coupling and harness support bracket clip-nut, between fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and inspecting for adequate clearance between hydraulic system and fuel vent tube with applicable on-condition actions.
The estimated cost for on-condition actions (replacement of hydraulic system support brackets) is $5,772 per product, consisting of 14 work-hours at $85 per hour ($1,190) plus $4,582 in parts.
FAA AD 2026-20-09 addresses low clearance conditions in the right wing of certain Bombardier BD-700-2A12 airplanes.
The effective date of FAA AD 2026-20-09 is November 18, 2026.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response:
The Office of Personnel Management issued a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act regulations to incorporate statutory amendments enacted in 2021 and 2023.  
The rule makes virtually all Federal civilian service, including temporary or intermittent service, qualifying service for determining FMLA eligibility and related paid parental leave eligibility.  
It also allows certain honorable active military service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement.  
In addition, the rule clarifies that annual and sick leave provided under authorities outside title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave and excludes certain Veterans Health Administration employees from title 5 FMLA coverage.  
The rule is scheduled to become effective December 14, 2026, unless OPM receives significant adverse comments by November 16, 2026, in which case OPM may withdraw the affected provisions and issue a proposed rule.

claim_breakdown.claim: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) issued a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations.
The direct final rule incorporates statutory amendments that were enacted in 2021 and 2023.
The OPM rule makes virtually all Federal civilian service, including temporary or intermittent service, qualifying service for determining FMLA eligibility.
The OPM rule makes virtually all Federal civilian service, including temporary or intermittent service, qualifying service for determining paid parental leave eligibility.
The OPM rule allows certain honorable active military service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month FMLA service requirement.
The OPM rule clarifies that annual and sick leave provided under authorities outside title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave.
The OPM rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration employees from title 5 FMLA coverage.
The OPM rule is scheduled to become effective on December 14, 2026.
The effective date of December 14, 2026, applies unless OPM receives significant adverse comments by November 16, 2026.
If OPM receives significant adverse comments by November 16, 2026, OPM may withdraw the affected provisions and issue a proposed rule.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Office of Personnel Management is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate statutory amendments from January 2021 and December 2023.
The rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026.
The statutory changes make virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility.
The rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage.

The December 2023 amendment allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility, but does not include service in the Coast Guard or commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.
The minimum qualifying service for FMLA eligibility under title 5 is 12 months.
